planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade sheltered from harsh winter wind; flower buds form in fall and hold through winter, so time any shaping cuts for right after bloom, not late summer.

directions: This selection carries the same tiered, architectural branching and large blue-green leaves as the species, but the fragrant, tubular winter flowers open in striking shades of orange to deep red-orange rather than the species' typical gold, held in rounded clusters against silvery bud casings through the cold months. Site it as a specimen in a shaded courtyard or woodland-edge bed where the unusual bloom color and rich fragrance can be enjoyed up close in late winter before leaves emerge. Give it consistent moisture during establishment and a wind-sheltered position, since flower buds and stem tips can suffer damage at the colder edge of its range. Avoid heavy pruning after midsummer, as next year's flower buds are already set by early fall.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; this selection blooms a bit later than the typical species, which can help buds dodge a hard late-winter freeze in colder gardens.

directions: A pure-white-flowered selection of paperbush, producing the same rounded clusters of intensely fragrant, tubular blooms from silvery, fur-covered buds, but in creamy white rather than gold, set against the same bold tiered branching and soft blue-green summer foliage. The clean white bloom color reads especially well against dark evergreen backdrops or in a shaded winter garden viewed from indoors. Plant in rich, evenly moist soil out of drying winter wind, and resist pruning after midsummer since flower buds for the following winter are already forming by then. Established plants tolerate short dry spells but perform best with supplemental water during summer heat.
sources: Plant Delights Nursery / JLBG plant introductions

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring or fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; this species tolerates drier soil than native American spicebush and holds its marcescent winter foliage best in a site sheltered from strong wind.

directions: This East Asian relative of common spicebush is grown chiefly for its exceptional fall and winter foliage display: the narrow, willow-like leaves turn a rich blend of orange, russet, and rust-red in autumn and, unlike most deciduous shrubs, persist on the stem through much of winter (marcescence) before finally dropping in spring, giving multi-season interest in an otherwise bare shade border. Small pale-yellow flowers appear on bare wood in very early spring, well before the leaves, offering an early nectar source for emerging pollinators. It is notably more tolerant of average, well-drained garden soil than L. benzoin, which prefers consistent moisture, making it a useful option for drier woodland-edge sites. Prune lightly, if at all, right after flowering to preserve the natural upright, twiggy form.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; dioecious, so plant a male and female together if fruit and seed set are desired.

directions: A larger, more tree-like relative of native spicebush, distinguished by broad, three-lobed leaves resembling a shallow maple leaf and a naturally rounded, small-tree habit that can eventually reach small-tree stature in ideal conditions. Clusters of small yellow flowers open on bare stems in earliest spring ahead of the foliage, followed on female plants by glossy black fruit favored by birds in fall. Its standout feature is dependable clear-gold to butter-yellow fall color, generally more consistent and vivid than the mixed yellow-to-orange color of American spicebush. Best used as an understory specimen or large shrub border anchor in a partially shaded woodland garden with rich, evenly moist soil; it accepts full shade but colors and flowers more heavily with some dappled sun.
